title: Grace Hopper: Pioneer of Computer Programming
summary: How Grace Hopper, a math teacher who joined the Navy, helped build early computers, created tools that let people write programs in plain words, and gave computer science the word "bug."
poll: Finding and fixing mistakes is just as important as writing new code.

versions.title: Grace and the Moth in the Machine
versions.text:
Grace Hopper was born in 1906. She lived in New York. Her mom let her try new things. Grace liked to fix clocks.

She took apart old clocks. She broke a few. She did not stop. She wanted to see how they worked. Grace loved math too.

A big war broke out. Grace joined the Navy. The Navy had a new machine. It did math fast. It was one of the first computers. Grace was glad. She wished to learn it all.

Grace helped write steps for it. The steps told it what to do. One day it broke. This was a problem. Her crew found a moth stuck in it! They called this a bug. We still say bug today.

Grace had one more big idea. She helped make a new way to write steps. It used real words, not just numbers.

Grace stayed in the Navy a long time. She still worked when she was old. Folks called her Amazing Grace.

versions.title: Grace and the Moth in the Machine

Grace Hopper was born in New York in 1906. As a kid, she liked to fix things. She took apart clocks. She wanted to see the gears. When one broke, her mom let her try again.

Grace loved math a lot. She went to college. She learned math and science there. Then she became a math teacher.

A big war began. Grace wanted to help. She joined the Navy. The Navy sent her to work on a new computer machine. It could solve math fast. It did sums much faster than a person.

Grace helped write the steps for it. One day, it stopped working. Her team looked inside. They found a moth stuck in a part! From then on, they called this problem a bug. People still use that word today.

Later, Grace helped build a new tool. It let people write steps with real words, not just numbers. This made it easier for more people to write programs.

Grace stayed in the Navy for many years. She kept working even when she was old. People gave her a nickname. They called her Amazing Grace.

From then on, people called any computer problem a bug, and programmers still use that word today.

Later in her career, Grace helped build an important innovation called a compiler, which let people write computer instructions using plain English words instead of long strings of numbers. This innovation made it far easier for many more people, not just trained mathematicians, to write their own programs.

Grace stayed in the Navy for decades and kept working long past the age when most people retire, even after she turned seventy, which amazed many younger sailors who served with her, and she eventually reached the rank of rear admiral, becoming one of the oldest active-duty officers in the Navy. The Navy sent her to Harvard University, where she worked on an enormous new machine called the Mark I, one of the very first large-scale electromechanical computers ever built, and it could solve long, intricate math problems much faster and more accurately than any person could possibly manage by hand.

From then on, people called any computer problem a bug, and programmers around the world still use that exact word today.

This innovation, which eventually contributed to a business programming language called COBOL, made it far easier for many more people, not only trained mathematicians, to write their own working programs.

Grace remained in the Navy for decades and continued working long past the age when most people retire, even after she turned seventy, which genuinely amazed many younger sailors who served alongside her, and she eventually reached the rank of rear admiral, becoming one of the oldest active-duty officers in the Navy. versions.title: Grace Hopper: Pioneer of Computer Programming
versions.text:
Grace Hopper was born in New York City in 1906. As a child, she was endlessly curious about how mechanical devices functioned, and she once dismantled seven alarm clocks in her family's house simply to study their internal gears. Her mother permitted her to keep experimenting, even after she broke several of them along the way, because she firmly believed that curiosity should always be encouraged in children, especially daughters, at a time when few people shared that particular conviction.

Grace loved mathematics from a remarkably young age, which was fairly unusual for girls during that era. She studied mathematics and physics at Vassar College, and she subsequently earned a doctorate in mathematics from Yale before becoming a professor who taught students for many years at a college located near New York City.

When World War II began, Grace wanted to serve her country, so she joined a branch of the Navy that specifically trained women, known as the WAVES, for important technical and scientific work. The Navy assigned her to Harvard University, where she worked on an enormous new machine called the Mark I, one of the very first large-scale electromechanical computers ever constructed. It could solve long, intricate mathematical problems far faster and more accurately than any person could possibly manage by hand.

Grace helped compose the long, precise sequences of instructions the computer needed to follow in order to operate correctly, carefully checking each individual step for possible errors. One day, a different computer her team worked on suddenly stopped functioning, and the team searched methodically through its many mechanical relays to determine the cause. They eventually discovered an actual moth trapped inside one of these delicate relays, which had caused the whole machine to malfunction; the team taped the moth into their logbook and noted that they had been "debugging" the machine. From that day forward, people began referring to any computer problem as a bug, and programmers around the world still use that exact term today.

Later in her career, Grace helped develop an important tool, known as a compiler, that translated plain English words into the numeric code a computer could actually execute, rather than requiring every single instruction to be written in confusing strings of numbers. This significant innovation, which eventually contributed to a widely used business programming language called COBOL, made it far easier for many more people, not only trained mathematicians, to write their own working programs; she also liked to explain how fast electricity moves by handing people a length of wire exactly as long as the distance electricity travels in one nanosecond.

Grace remained in the Navy for decades and continued working long after most people choose to retire, even after she turned seventy years old, which genuinely amazed many younger sailors who served alongside her, and she eventually reached the rank of rear admiral, becoming one of the oldest active-duty officers in the entire Navy. People around the world, including many students in Saudi Arabia who now study computer science, gave her a warm, lasting nickname: Amazing Grace.

versions.title: Grace Hopper: Pioneer of Computer Programming
versions.text:
Grace Hopper entered the world in New York City in the year 1906. As a child, she displayed an endless and insatiable curiosity about precisely how mechanical devices functioned, and she once methodically dismantled seven alarm clocks in her family's house purely to study their intricate internal gears in considerable detail. Her mother permitted her to keep experimenting, even after she inadvertently broke several of the clocks along the way, because she firmly and genuinely believed that intellectual curiosity ought always to be actively encouraged in children, including daughters, during an era when remarkably few people shared that particular conviction.

Grace developed a deep and abiding passion for mathematics from a remarkably young age, which was fairly unusual for girls during that restrictive historical era. She studied mathematics and physics rigorously at Vassar College, and she subsequently earned a doctorate in mathematics from Yale University before becoming a highly respected professor who instructed students for many years at a college situated near New York City.

When World War II erupted across the globe, Grace felt an overwhelming desire to serve her country, so she enlisted in a specialized branch of the Navy that specifically trained women, known by the designation WAVES, for important technical and scientific work. The Navy assigned her to Harvard University, where she was placed on a team working on an enormous new machine called the Mark I, one of the very first large-scale electromechanical computers ever constructed anywhere in the world. This remarkable machine could solve exceedingly long, intricate mathematical problems far faster and more accurately than any human being could conceivably manage by hand.

Grace helped compose the long, meticulously precise sequences of instructions the computer needed to follow in order to operate correctly, painstakingly checking each individual step for any possible errors. One day, a different computer her team worked on suddenly ceased functioning entirely, and the team searched methodically through its many mechanical relays to determine the underlying cause of the failure. They eventually discovered an actual moth trapped inside one of these delicate relays, which had caused the entire machine to malfunction; the team taped the moth directly into their official logbook and noted, with some amusement, that they had spent the afternoon "debugging" the machine. From that day forward, people throughout the computing world began referring to any computer problem as a bug, and programmers around the entire globe still use that exact term today.

Later in her distinguished and lengthy career, Grace helped develop an important and influential tool, known as a compiler, that translated plain English words into the numeric code a computer could actually execute, rather than requiring every single instruction to be laboriously written out in confusing strings of numbers. This significant innovation, which eventually contributed substantially to the development of a widely used business programming language called COBOL, made it far easier for many more people, not merely trained mathematicians, to write their own functioning programs; she also enjoyed explaining how remarkably fast electricity travels by handing curious visitors a length of wire exactly as long as the distance electricity travels in a single nanosecond.

Grace remained in active Navy service for several decades and continued working long after most people choose to retire, even well after she turned seventy years old, which genuinely astonished many younger sailors who served alongside her, and she eventually attained the distinguished rank of rear admiral, becoming one of the oldest active-duty officers in the entire United States Navy. People around the world, including many students in Saudi Arabia who now diligently study computer science, affectionately gave her a warm, lasting nickname that endures to this day: Amazing Grace.

HIGH.prompt: Grace Hopper's work connected careful technical instructions with the needs of ordinary people who were not mathematicians. Explain why her work still matters today, using the words innovation and mechanical.
checklist: I explained what Grace built and why it counts as an innovation.
I used innovation and mechanical correctly.
I connected her ideas to programming today.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Grace Hopper's work still matters today because her compiler, a true innovation, translated plain English words into the code a computer could run, instead of forcing every programmer to write confusing strings of numbers by hand. This change opened programming to far more people, not only trained mathematicians, and helped lead to COBOL, a widely used programming language. Over her career, Grace also gave the field the word bug, after her team found a moth inside a mechanical relay, a term programmers around the world still use whenever they fix a problem in their code today.
